title: How to Choose a CAS Project With Real Community…
summary: Learn how to choose a CAS project with real community impact, verify an authentic need, build partnerships, measure results, and plan your fall term.
body_markdown:
To **choose a CAS project with real community impact** , begin with a verified community need rather than an activity you assume people will value. Speak with those affected, identify a useful role for your team, and design a collaborative response that you can sustain and evaluate.


September-November offers a practical structure: investigate in September, prepare in October, then begin meaningful action and adjustment in November.


### What an IB CAS project must involve


A CAS project is more than a large volunteer activity. According to the[IB's official CAS project guidance](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/creativity-activity-and-service/cas-projects/) , every Diploma Programme student must complete at least one CAS project.


Official IB guidance describes it as a **collaborative series of sequential CAS experiences lasting at least one month** . It may address Creativity, Activity, Service, or any combination of the three strands. Contrary to a common misconception, one project does not have to include every strand.


A suitable project should include:


- Collaboration with students, community members, or both
- Connected experiences rather than one isolated event
- At least one month from initiation to completion
- Purposeful planning, action, reflection, and evidence
- Opportunities for challenge and personal development


When Service is involved, the response should address an **authentic community need** through reciprocal engagement. The[IB overview of Creativity, Activity, Service](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/creativity-activity-and-service/) also emphasizes initiative, perseverance, collaboration, problem-solving, and decision-making.


Your school decides whether a proposal is appropriate. Obtain approval from your CAS coordinator before spending money, collecting personal information, or promising support to an organisation.


### Start with a need, not an event


Students frequently begin with an event such as a fundraiser, clothing drive, awareness account, or tutoring club. A stronger starting question is: **What does this community identify as a priority, and what useful role can our team play?**


A community may be a school group, neighbourhood, care home, environmental organisation, sports club, or online community. Impact does not require national scale. Reliable homework support for 12 younger students may be more valuable than a large campaign producing no observable benefit.


Investigate by interviewing an informed representative, consulting potential participants, observing existing provision, and reviewing reliable local information. Ask what has already been attempted and which practical, cultural, or ethical constraints must shape your response.


The IB's[service learning stages resource](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/brochures-and-infographics/pdfs/sl-stages-en.pdf) connects investigation, preparation, action, reflection, and demonstration. These stages help prevent students from rushing into action based on assumptions.


### Use a five-part project test


Compare each possible project against five criteria.


Test Question to ask


Need Has the intended community confirmed that this matters?


Partnership Will community members influence goals and decisions?


Feasibility Can the team deliver safely with available time and resources?


Learning Will the work create genuine challenge and collaboration?


Impact Can the team observe a useful change without exaggeration?


Reject ideas that depend mainly on assumptions. Generic mental-health posters, for example, may appear helpful, but a counsellor or qualified organisation should advise what information is needed, which language is appropriate, and where students can obtain professional support.


Feasibility matters as much as ambition. A focused six-week reading programme with reliable attendance is stronger than a proposed city-wide literacy campaign that never moves beyond social media.


### Plan your IB CAS fall term


A realistic **IB CAS fall term** plan leaves time for investigation and partnership before action.


Period Main task Useful evidence


Early September List interests, skills, communities, and constraints Personal inventory and initial ideas


Late September Contact partners and investigate needs Emails, interview notes, observations, or surveys


October Agree on goals, roles, safeguarding, and measures Approved proposal, timeline, budget, and risk plan


November Deliver initial action, collect feedback, and adjust Attendance, anonymised feedback, work samples, and reflections


Plan around academic deadlines from the outset. RevisionDojo's guide to[balancing CAS with academics](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-balance-cas-with-academics-and-social-life) can help you set manageable weekly commitments. The one-month requirement covers the connected project process, not necessarily four identical action sessions.


### Define impact before taking action


**Outputs** describe what your team delivered. **Outcomes** describe what changed. Four tutoring sessions are an output; greater participant confidence with specified skills may be an outcome.


Choose one modest outcome and establish a baseline. Before digital-skills sessions, for example, ask participants which tasks they can complete independently, then repeat the questions afterwards. Attendance, participant feedback, completed products, observed skill development, and requests to continue may provide useful evidence.


Do not claim that a small project “solved” poverty, isolation, or climate change. Honest evidence of a limited contribution is more credible and ethically responsible than unsupported claims.


### Design with the community and collect useful evidence


Real impact depends on **reciprocity** . Partners should help define the goal, methods, timing, accessibility, safeguarding arrangements, consent procedures, and appropriate measures of success. They should also influence adjustments when feedback shows that something is not working.


For example, do not independently collect donations and assume they will help. Ask an organisation which items are needed, in what condition, and how distribution operates. Sorting, transport, translation, or targeted purchasing may be more useful than collecting large quantities of unsuitable goods.


Your CAS portfolio is not formally graded, but it should demonstrate engagement and progress toward the seven learning outcomes. RevisionDojo's guide to[CAS projects and experiences](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-counts-as-a-cas-project-vs-a-cas-experience) explains why sustained collaboration differs from a one-off activity.


Useful evidence includes meeting notes, changing plans, role allocations, partner feedback, drafts, attendance records, anonymised responses, and photographs taken with appropriate consent. Reflect when something significant occurs, such as conflict, an ethical concern, an unexpected result, or a change of plan. The guide to[meaningful CAS reflections](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-cas-reflections-what-coordinators-want) shows how to move beyond description.


### Common mistakes that weaken impact


Avoid choosing an impressive cause without local evidence, measuring visibility instead of benefit, or asking a partner merely to approve a finished plan. Views and poster numbers are outputs, not proof that understanding or behaviour changed.


Plan a responsible ending by transferring resources, documenting procedures, identifying a successor, or explaining why the work will stop. Do not force all seven learning outcomes into one project; connect reflections only to outcomes genuinely supported by evidence.


### Conclusion


Choose a CAS project by verifying a need, working collaboratively, setting a feasible goal, and distinguishing outputs from outcomes. A small project designed with a community can have more responsible impact than an ambitious project based on assumptions.


RevisionDojo's[CAS project ideas and planning guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/cas-project-experience-ideas-unleash-your-creativity-activity-and-service) can help you compare manageable formats, while its reflection guidance can help you document meaningful decisions throughout the project.
